sources.title: Cyril Toumanoff, BAGRATIDS, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Direct and indexed scholarly text read: Georgian branch, united kingdom in 1008, partition into three kingdoms by the end of the fifteenth century. Debated early dynastic origins not adopted.

sources.title: Keith Hitchins, GEORGIA II. History of Iranian-Georgian Relations, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Direct scholarly text read, medieval unification and golden age, Mongol invasions from the 1220s, later revivals, late fifteenth-century division into Kartli, Kakheti, Imereti and Samtskhe-Saatabago; sixteenth-century Ottoman/Safavid competition. No claim that all Georgian communities shared one identity.

sources.title: British Council and Georgian National Museum, King David IV: 2019 coin exhibition
sources.note: Direct full page read, Early Life and coin provenance/description sections. Uses 1089 accession, royal centralization, 1103 council and political coin imagery. Avoids inflated military numbers, problematic academy foundation list and inconsistent Tbilisi capture dating in this page.

sources.title: Encyclopedia, T’amar Bagrationi: medieval royal portraits (2022)
sources.note: Original publisher indexed text and figure captions read; direct fetch returned 429. Figures 1-5 identify inscribed portraits, Vardzia 1180s with father and later images with husband/heir. Article and numismatic catalogue prefer 1210 death; other authorities use 1213, so no exact death year adopted.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Gelati Monastery
sources.note: Full institutional description read: foundation 1106, main church completion 1130, stone architecture, twelfth-century mosaic; academy translations by Ioane Petritzi and Arsen Ikaltoeli; scriptorium location unknown and surviving twelfth-century Gospel.

sources.title: Georgian National Academy of Sciences, Dmanisi Archaeological Site
sources.note: Direct full text read: medieval town, archaeology from 1936, paved streets, baths, barns, wine cellars, mosque and madrasa, pottery/glass production. Conflicting statements about most coins being Georgian versus foreign are omitted. Prehistoric hominin occupation not merged with medieval kingdom.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Upper Svaneti
sources.note: Direct full description read: Chazhashi medieval tower houses, lower hall with hearth and wood partition for humans/livestock, insulating corridor, seasonal upstairs residence, storage and tower access. Domestic arrangements describe surviving Svan tradition of medieval origin, not a securely dated universal twelfth-century household.

sources.title: Ministry of Culture of Georgia, Vardzia-Khertvisi tentative-list submission
sources.note: Direct state-party submission read: description paragraphs 1-4 and final landscape paragraph; twelfth/thirteenth-century Vardzia, cave cells/dwellings, inscriptions, mural portraits and terraced village/arable landscape. A tentative listing, not an inscribed World Heritage property.

sources.title: Georgian National Centre of Manuscripts, Medical and Veterinary Manuscripts catalogue
sources.note: Original institutional PDF indexed text read; direct URL redirects to redesigned homepage. Reproducible queries combine exact URL with "13th" and "Q 877". Medical palimpsest S 4939 lower layer folios 25v-28r, palaeographically thirteenth century; fifteenth-century Q 877, Zaza of Panaskerti, folios 1-24r general medicine then organ-specific conditions. Treatments described only as historical knowledge.

sources.title: Tbilisi State University, coins of Giorgi IV with the legend Giorgi, son of Tamar
sources.note: Original institutional catalogue indexed text independently rechecked with query site:geonumismatics.tsu.ge "Giorgi, son of Tamar" "430"; direct fetch returns 502. Obverse exact Asomtavruli legend and English gloss, K’oronikon 430 equivalent 1210. Shared scholarly commentary on irregular copper appears across types 64-72; treated as one source budget. Does not assume every coin was produced in its inscribed date or settle disputed Tamar death year.

proposedOverrides.name: Kingdom of Georgia
proposedOverrides.summary: The medieval Georgian kingdom united under Bagrat III and flourished under David IV and Tamar, before later fragmentation.

batchIdentityNotes.identity: Medieval united Georgian kingdom under Bagrationi rulers, followed by its fragmentation; not the modern Republic of Georgia or every earlier Caucasian polity.
batchIdentityNotes.region: Asia, following current coverage geographicQueueHints; Caucasus cross-regional location explained in public overview.
batchIdentityNotes.mapEvidence: identity.json decodes nine polygons from world-1000 through world-1500. Broad changing Caucasus outlines, including a small detached world-1000 feature. Imported start precedes 1008 unification and end follows late-fifteenth-century fragmentation. No exact historic frontier or ethnic homogeneity claimed.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Periods 1490 boundary approximate shorthand for late-fifteenth-century transition, explicitly qualified. No exact Tamar death year because authorities differ between 1210 and1213. Coin inscribed1210 not treated as universal minting date. Svan household traditions explicitly qualified, not assigned invented point years.
batchIdentityNotes.limits: No universal schooling, effective medieval treatment or toilet/sewer system claimed. Baths, regional household partitions, schools and medical manuscripts supply the supported everyday-life evidence. Modern disputed political boundaries are not adjudicated.
